column1: #tags column:3
Name the three programs of the case study and say what data each one keeps.
column2: The Web UI, `cmd/web`, has four PostgreSQL tables. The evaluator, `cmd/eval`, has files: datasets and a results folder for each evaluator run. The scripted agent, `cmd/test-agent`, has nothing lasting, only sessions in memory.

column1: How does the evaluator reach the Web UI, and what does it know of the agent and the database?
column2: Through a browser that it drives: the browser sends the requests. Of the agent and the database it knows nothing; neither appears in its code.

column1: Which packages may a package under `internal/core` import, and what happens when it imports something else?
column2: Only the domain and the port packages, besides most of the standard library. Any other import makes `TestDependencies` fail, and the failure names the file, the import and the rule.

column1: How do `chat.Service`, `adkrest.Client` and `wire` each relate to the port `AgentGateway`? Give one verb for each.
column2: `chat.Service` *calls* the port, `adkrest.Client` *implements* it, and `wire` *passes* the client to the service.

column1: Which of the two requests of a message makes the Web UI call the agent, and through which use case method and port method?
column2: The GET, `GET /c/{id}/m/{mid}/stream`. Its handler reaches `Chat.Stream`, and that method calls `AgentGateway.Run`.

column1: Which status does the stored reply have right after the POST, while the stream runs, and after a run that ends with text and no error?
column2: First `pending`, then `streaming` once the stream has claimed the reply, and `complete` at the end of such a run.

column1: Name the five statuses of a reply and say which of them are final.
column2: A reply is pending, streaming, complete, stopped or failed. The last three are final.

column1: Which layer lets a reply move from pending to streaming, and how does it let only one of several concurrent callers through?
column2: The store: `Claim` is one UPDATE that requires the status pending, so only one caller changes a row.

column1: During a run the agent cannot be reached. Which sentence does the reader see, and where does the technical detail go?
column2: The reader sees "The agent can't be reached right now. Try again in a moment." The cause itself is written to the log and never shown.

column1: Why does `errors.Is` say that `TooLong(500)` matches `ErrMessageTooLong` although the two values differ?
column2: `ValidationError.Is` compares only the code, and `TooLong(500)` carries the same code as `ErrMessageTooLong`, although its message differs.

column1: How do the chat use case and the PostgreSQL store each relate to the `MessageStore` port? Give a verb for each link.
column2: The use case *uses* the port, and the PostgreSQL store *implements* it.

column1: Why is `MessageStore` declared in a shared port package and not inside the package of the chat use case?
column2: More than one use case needs it: the chat service and the conversation service are both given a `MessageStore`, so its port is written once, where both can import it.

column1: A reply is `streaming` in the store. What does `Stream` yield when this process has a run for it, and what does it yield when it has none?
column2: With a run, only `ErrAlreadyStreaming`. With none, it treats the reply as lost, repairs it, and yields one `done` event with the repaired state.

column1: After the text "par", the agent's stream ends with an error that wraps `ErrIncompleteStream`. Which status and which sentence does the store keep?
column2: Status `failed`, with the sentence "The agent's answer was cut off."

column1: Why must the claim ignore the cancellation of the request, and what limit does it get?
column2: A claim can be committed just as the caller leaves; if nobody finishes it, the reply stays streaming. The limit is five seconds.

column1: A Stop arrives for a streaming reply whose save is very slow. What does `Stop` return, and after how long at most?
column2: The reply as stored, which can still say `streaming`, after at most nine seconds.

column1: How does Lost-Run Repair use the registry, and how does `Stop` use the registry and the repair?
column2: The repair takes a missing run in the registry as its evidence that nothing writes the reply. `Stop` uses the registry to find the run to cancel, and falls back to the repair when it finds none.

column1: A stream connects while a Stop is between its claim and its save of an unstarted reply. What does the stream get, and how does the reply end?
column2: `ErrAlreadyStreaming`: Stop put itself in the registry as the writer, so the stream is turned away. The reply ends as `stopped`.

column1: When does the gateway create a session, and which call does it make right after the creation?
column2: Only when the answer to a turn is a 404 that says the session was not found. Right after, it sends the same turn a second time.

column1: Which HTTP request is the ping, and what must the answer hold for the ping to succeed?
column2: A GET of `/list-apps`. The list in the answer must include the app that the settings name.

column1: An ADK event that is not partial holds a reasoning part and a text part. What does the gateway make of them?
column2: The text part becomes a final event. The reasoning part is dropped.

column1: A stream ends cleanly after three deltas, with no final event. Which error does the gateway yield, and which sentence does the reader see?
column2: `ErrIncompleteStream`. The reader sees "The agent's answer was cut off."

column1: Which error does `Run` yield when the context of the caller ends, and what does `classify` check first?
column2: `context.Canceled`. `classify` looks at the caller's own context before anything else.

column1: What does the chat use case do with the errors that the gateway yields?
column2: The first error goes to its outcome table. The table picks the status and the fixed sentence of the reply.

column1: Which rule about the status of a message does the schema enforce, and which rule about the same column is left to the SQL statements?
column2: A CHECK constraint admits only the five status values. Which value may follow which is not in the schema: the guards of the methods that change a status keep that order.

column1: Twenty requests add a message to one conversation at once. How does `AppendPair` keep the numbers free of gaps, and what happens to the requests that do not win?
column2: The row lock of the conversation comes before the read of the highest number, so one request numbers at a time. One wins; the other nineteen find an unfinished reply and get `ErrInvalidState`.

column1: Two tabs claim the same pending reply at the same moment. Why does only one claim win, and what does the other tab receive?
column2: The claim is one `UPDATE` that requires the status `pending`. The second `UPDATE` waits for the first, tests its condition again, finds `streaming` and changes no row. That tab gets `ErrAlreadyStreaming`.

column1: How do the Compare-and-Set Claim and Recover at Startup depend on each other? Answer with two verbs.
column2: The claim leaves a reply `streaming` with no expiry, so a crash strands it. Recover at Startup closes such a reply as failed when the process starts again.

column1: `Finish` finds that its update changed no row. Why does it read the table once more, and what can that read tell it?
column2: A count of zero does not say which condition failed. One `SELECT EXISTS` tells the two causes apart: no such message, which is `ErrNotFound`, or a message that is not streaming, which is `ErrInvalidState`.

column1: Name the layers that `Handler` puts around the route table, from the outside in.
column2: `RequestID`, `AccessLog`, `Recover`, `SecurityHeaders`, `Deadlines`, the cross-origin check and `MaxBody`.

column1: Why does the access log stand outside the layer that recovers from panics?
column2: From outside, its line holds the 500 that the recovering layer sends after a handler panics.

column1: An anonymous visitor asks for a path that no route has. What does the Web UI answer, and why is it not a 404?
column2: It redirects to the sign-in page with a 303, as for any private page. A path is public only when `isPublic` lists it, and this one is not listed.

column1: A key may make 3 requests at once and gains 2 tokens a second. It has just used all 3. When does its next request pass, and what does a refused request get back?
column2: After 500 ms. A refused request gets a 429 answer with a `Retry-After` header.

column1: How do `Deadlines` and `MaxBody` depend on each other? Answer with verbs.
column2: `MaxBody` replaces the body of every request, even a GET. `Deadlines` sets its read deadline only on a request that has a body, so it must stand outside `MaxBody`.

column1: What does the database keep in place of a session token, and why can a copy of the sessions table not take over a session?
column2: It stores a digest of the token, never the token. A digest sent as the cookie fails, because the server hashes the cookie value again before it searches.

column1: An attacker signs in with an email that has no account, then with a real account and a wrong password. Why do the two look the same?
column2: For the email without an account the server still verifies the typed password, against a decoy hash, so both sign-ins cost one hash. Both then get the same error and the same message.

column1: A script and a person's browser both ask for a private page without being signed in. What does each one receive?
column2: The script receives status 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. The person's browser receives a 303 redirect to the sign-in page.

column1: What does an anonymous event stream receive when its session is gone, and why does the server not redirect it?
column2: It receives status 200 and a stream with a failed reply that says the session has ended, then a done event. After a redirect the event-stream extension would reconnect without end.

column1: Which cookie flag keeps scripts from reading the session cookie, and what does SameSite=Lax prevent?
column2: HttpOnly keeps scripts away from the cookie. With SameSite=Lax the browser does not attach the cookie to a POST that another site starts.

column1: How do the security headers and the cross-origin check depend on their order in the middleware chain?
column2: The header layer wraps the cross-origin layer, so a request that the cross-origin layer refuses still gets the security headers on its answer.

column1: A reply holds a block `<script>alert(1)</script>` and a link `[open](javascript:alert(1))`. What does the reader see for each?
column2: The script block shows up as plain characters, tags included, and does not run. Of the link, only the word open is left, as text with no link around it.

column1: Does the sanitizer rely on the converter to keep the page safe, and how does a test show it?
column2: No. One test hands hostile HTML to the policy directly, with no converter in front of it, and each case comes out harmless.

column1: What does the size cap protect, and what does the reader see when a reply is over it?
column2: The CPU of the server: one huge reply would otherwise be converted again at each stream update. Past the cap, the reader gets the complete text escaped as plain text in a `pre` block.

column1: What does the render cache protect, and why does a reply that is still being written never enter it?
column2: The cost of showing a conversation, where each reply would otherwise be rendered again. An unfinished reply has a different text at each snapshot, so its text is rendered without being kept.

column1: Why does highlighting write CSS classes and not inline styles, and where does the stylesheet for the classes come from?
column2: The Content Security Policy of the page forbids inline styles. The stylesheet is generated: `ChromaCSS` builds it, and it is committed as `chroma.css`.

column1: In which goroutine does the iterator of `Service.Stream` run, and which function holds the loop that decides when a snapshot is written to the browser?
column2: In the goroutine that `feed` starts. The loop is in `pump`, which asks the pacer whether to send.

column1: With a base interval of 50 ms and a last update that cost 30 ms, what is the shortest time before the next update, and why?
column2: It is 120 ms: the interval is whichever is larger, the base or four times the cost of the last update.

column1: The agent breaks off after part of a reply was shown. What does the stream send next, and which HTTP status did it answer with?
column2: One last update that shows the reply as failed, with the text that arrived and one fixed sentence, and then a `done` event. The status was 200.

column1: How do the contexts of a stream depend on each other, and what does a shutdown of the server end?
column2: The run's context is derived from the client's, so a client that leaves ends both. The shutdown context cancels only the run's, so a shutdown ends the run and the stream stays open to send the stopped reply.

column1: Why does the stream answer 200 even for a reply that does not exist?
column2: The SSE extension of the page opens a stream again after any HTTP error, without end. So the stream answers 200 and carries the refusal inside it.

column1: The server accepts a message that the reader sends in an open conversation. What does the answer hold, and where does htmx put each part?
column2: Two bubbles, the reader's message and the wrapper of the reply, and an element for the composer's message line. htmx appends the bubbles at the end of the list. It swaps the last element over the message line by its id.

column1: The server refuses a send with status 409. Which two things in the answer leave the conversation on screen as it is?
column2: The header `HX-Reswap: none`, and a body that holds only the out-of-band message line.

column1: A reply is streaming. The reader scrolls 300 pixels up from the end, and more text arrives. What happens to the view, and what appears?
column2: The view stays where it is, because 300 pixels is more than the tolerance of 80 pixels. The button "Jump to latest" appears.

column1: The reader has scrolled far up and then sends a message that the server accepts. Where is the view afterwards, and which value causes that?
column2: At the end of the list. Sending sets `forceFollow`, and the next change of the list then follows whatever the scroll position is.

column1: What kind of files import the contract table, and which three places hold the contract version?
column2: Three test files, and no production file. The version is the literal on the body in the base template, the constant `contract.Version`, and the evaluator's own constant `SupportedContract`.

column1: How do `checkContract` and `TestUIContract_NoticesDamage` depend on each other? Give one verb for each direction.
column2: The damage test uses `checkContract` as its judge. In return it proves that `checkContract` can see a fault.

column1: A user message holds both `#slow` and `#error`, and the model has no fixture. What does the scripted agent answer, and what decides it?
column2: An error. `#error` comes before `#slow` in the fixed order in which the model goes through its keywords, and the earliest keyword of that order wins.

column1: A fixture reply has `fail_first` 1. One question is asked twice, then a reworded question that names the same id. What comes back each time?
column2: An error the first time and the text the second time. The reworded question gets an error again.

column1: Which responses does the model yield, in order, for a streamed `#think` reply, and which of them carries the token counts?
column2: A partial response that holds the reasoning part, then a partial response for every chunk of the text, and last the aggregated response. The token counts come with the aggregated response and with no other.

column1: How does a test prove that the model stopped when the client left?
column2: It cancels its own request and then waits until `Cancelled`, the count of calls that were cut short in the model that the test holds, reads 1.

column1: How do the two patterns of this chapter work together?
column2: The counters of Probe Counters sit inside the Scripted Model, which adds to them as it answers. A test keeps the model that it started and reads the counters from it.

column1: Which port gives a worker a new browser after one has died, and which adapter stands behind it?
column2: The port is `DriverFactory`, and the adapter that stands behind it is `devtools.Factory`.

column1: In an attempt that ends with a right answer, which happens first: scoring the answer or judging the UI checks? Name the driver call that begins each of the two steps.
column2: Scoring the answer comes first. It begins with the driver call `ReadRaw`, and judging the UI checks begins with `Collect`.

column1: Which two failures does an attempt hand up as an error instead of writing them into its row?
column2: The death of its driver, and the end of the context, which is a cancelled run.

column1: How do `fatal` and `Runner.worker` share the work when a browser dies during an attempt?
column2: `fatal` returns the error, so the attempt ends without a row. `Runner.worker` gets that error, starts another browser and asks the same slot once more; when the browser dies a second time, the worker writes a `driver_died` row itself.

column1: Ctrl-C stops a run while one attempt is still waiting for its reply. Which exit code does the program return, and does that attempt get a row?
column2: The program returns 130, and the attempt that was waiting gets no row.

column1: A finished run has a failed Must check and also an accuracy below `--min-accuracy`. Which exit code does it return, and why that one?
column2: It returns 2. In `judge` the first case that matches decides, and the case of a failed Must check comes before the case of the accuracy.

column1: The truth is `1,000` and the answer is `1000`. Which rule does `Question` apply, and what is the verdict?
column2: The list rule: with its comma the truth is no number but a list of `1` and `000`. The answer has only one element, so the verdict is false.

column1: What does `pyFloat` copy from Python, and what does `pyLower` copy?
column2: `pyFloat` reads a number from text by the grammar of Python's `float()`. `pyLower` puts text into lower case as Python's `str.lower()` does.

column1: A reply holds the marker twice. After the second one come a blank line and then `**7**`. What does `Extract` return, and by which rule?
column2: It returns `7`. Only the text behind the last marker counts; from it the rule takes the first line that is not empty and drops the `**` at both ends.

column1: Which of these three replies does `Extract` reject, and which status does that attempt get: `**FINAL ANSWER:** 42`, `FINAL ANSWER : 42`, `final answer: 42`?
column2: The second one. With a space in front of the colon the text is not the marker, so the attempt gets the status `no_final_answer`.

column1: How do the built-in prompt and `Extract` depend on each other, and what does `ParsePrompt` leave untested?
column2: The prompt asks the agent to end with the marker, and the marker is the only thing that `Extract` searches for. `ParsePrompt` tests that the question comes out; it does not test that a template names the marker.

column1: What must the command of the browser server look like for `CheckMCP` to accept it?
column2: It has to be npx followed by `chrome-devtools-mcp` at one exact version number. The arguments have to include four required flags.

column1: Which variables of the evaluator's environment does the server process receive, and which never?
column2: Only variables whose names are on an allow-list of names and prefixes. A name that resembles a secret is never passed.

column1: Why does a slow tool call not change the time to first text that the evaluator reports?
column2: Both times are recorded inside the page, on the page's own clock, at the moment each event happens. They are read afterwards, and the result is only their difference.

column1: Which error does `Session.Call` return when the tool ran and refused, and which when the call passed its own deadline?
column2: A `*ToolError` when the tool refused. An error wrapping `domain.ErrDriverDied` when the call went past its own deadline.

column1: The caller's context ends during a tool call. What does `Session.Call` return, and what happens to the session?
column2: It returns the caller's own context error. The session is not marked dead, so it can still be used.

column1: How do the driver and the run engine share the work when a browser is lost?
column2: The driver only signals the loss, with an error wrapping `ErrDriverDied`. The run engine does the restart: its worker opens a new browser, signs in and repeats the attempt one time.

column1: An attempt runs out of time and Stop is pressed. What does U-03 answer if the reply then reaches a final status, and what if it does not?
column2: `na` in the first case: the agent was slow, and the UI did end the reply. `fail` in the second.

column1: Which two things can `na` mean, and what happens to a Must check that only ever answered `na` in a run?
column2: Either the check did not apply, or the data to decide were missing. Its verdict is `na` too, and it is listed as undecided, never as passed.

column1: How do the browser adapter and the `Judge` functions depend on each other in a probe?
column2: The adapter measures in the browser and calls the judge with plain numbers and facts. The judge, a pure function in the core, decides the result from them and the thresholds.

column1: A probe returns an error. What does the suite record for it, and what happens to the probes after it?
column2: A not-applicable outcome with the reason, because the probe could not run. The later probes still run, unless the browser itself died.

column1: For 8 correct answers of 10 attempts, give the centre, the half-width and the two bounds of the 95% Wilson interval.
column2: The centre is about 0.717 and the half-width about 0.227, so the interval runs from about 49% to about 94%.

column1: Which two pairs of counts feed the accuracy intervals of the agent scorecard, and how do repeats enter them?
column2: Correct over attempted, and correct over eligible. Both count attempts, so the repeats of one problem enter as separate trials.

column1: The hub redirects a request for a file to a CDN on another host. Which requests carry the token, and what removes it before the last one?
column2: Two requests carry it, the one that fetches the listing and the hub's own leg of the download, because both addresses are configured. The client's `CheckRedirect` strips `Authorization` before the redirect to the CDN is followed.

column1: A run is killed while a row is being written. What does `--resume` do to the results file first, and which slots does it ask?
column2: `Begin` first mends the tail of `results.jsonl` and takes the cut row out. The run then asks each slot with no row and each slot whose newest row says `ui_error`.

column1: In which two cases does the Git Guard refuse a directory?
column2: When nothing ignores the directory, so that git would take it with the next commit, and when it is ignored but one of its files is tracked.

column1: How do `Store.Index` and the runner depend on each other when a run is resumed?
column2: The runner asks `Index` which slots are done and strikes them from its plan. `Index` can tell only because the runner's workers wrote a row for each attempt that ended.

column1: What does `Append` leave out of a row by default, and which settings does `run.json` never hold?
column2: The question, the expected answer and the agent's answer; they stay only with `--include-text`. `run.json` has no setting whose name reads like a secret, such as one with `token` in it.

column1: A second copy of the Web UI is started by mistake while the first one serves. At which step does it stop, and what has it done to the database by then?
column2: It stops at once when it asks for the port, which the first copy holds. By then it has done nothing to the database, because every database step comes after the port.

column1: Put these five startup steps in order: the recovery of interrupted replies, the port, the first user, the migrations, the database ping.
column2: The port, the database ping, the migrations, the recovery of interrupted replies, the first user.

column1: Your shell exports a variable, and `.env` holds another value for the same key. Which value does the Web UI use when you start the binary by hand, and which when `run.sh` starts it?
column2: By hand, the exported value: for the programs the environment beats the file. Through `run.sh`, the value of `.env`: the script loads the file into the environment over what was there.

column1: What does a `Secret` show when it is logged or written as JSON, and how does code get the real value?
column2: It shows the placeholder `[redacted]`. Code gets the value by calling `Reveal`.

column1: What does `docker compose up` start when no profile is named, and what does the profile `selftest` add?
column2: With no profile it starts PostgreSQL and the scripted agent. The profile `selftest` adds a second scripted agent with scripted answers and a Web UI that talks to that agent.

column1: How does the health check that Compose defines depend on what the web image contains?
column2: The image holds the binary and neither a shell nor curl. So Compose cannot call another program: its health check starts the binary itself with the argument `healthcheck`.

column1: What may a use case of the Web UI import, and what does the test print for any other import?
column2: Only the Web UI's domain and ports, plus the standard library without net/http, database/sql, os and io/fs. For any other import the test names the offending file, the import path and the plain sentence of the broken rule.

column1: The only directory that a rule names is deleted. Which test fails, and why does `TestDependencies` stay green?
column2: TestEveryRuleStillApplies fails, since that directory has no production file left. TestDependencies stays green because a rule without files has nothing to forbid.

column1: Which layer proves how a store behaves against a real database, and what does it need that the unit tests do not?
column2: The store suites under it/, which exercise the stores on a real PostgreSQL. They need Docker, and the unit tests do not.

column1: How does the leak check depend on the way the stack starts the Web UI?
column2: The stack starts the application as a goroutine inside the test process. So its goroutines appear in the same stack dump as the test's, the dump that the leak check searches.

column1: A change adds a package of 60 statements, and the unit tests execute 24. Both totals stay above their floors. Does the gate pass?
column2: No. The new package stands at 40 percent, under the 50 percent that every package must reach, so the gate fails unless COVER_EXEMPT lists it.
